opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is a really exciting time to be a founder, because the gap between a research paper and a usable product has never been shorter. A few things I'd say.

First, read papers not just for the headline result but for the failure modes. The limitations section is often where the real opportunities are hiding. When a lab publishes something and says "this works in simulation but transfer to the real world is still hard," or "this model is great at short-horizon tasks but falls apart over long horizons," that's basically a map of unsolved problems. Founders who can see that gap and say "I can close it for this specific domain" tend to find really defensible positions.

Second, treat open source as your starting line, not your finish line. Open-weight models, open simulators, open datasets have raised the floor for everyone. That means if your entire value proposition is "we fine-tuned an open model," that's going to commoditize very quickly. But if you use those tools to get to a working prototype in weeks instead of years, and then spend your energy on the things open source doesn't give you, like proprietary data, a tight feedback loop with real users, deployment in messy physical environments, then you've built something durable.

Third, and this is a bit of my bias coming from embodied AI, look at where the data doesn't exist yet. Language models had the internet. Robotics and a lot of physical-world applications don't have an internet-scale dataset lying around. So the question becomes: how do you generate it? Simulation, synthetic data, teleoperation, human video. Whoever builds the data flywheel in a vertical that doesn't have one yet is going to have an enormous advantage, and that's not something you can just download from Hugging Face.

And finally, I'd say be ambitious but time your bets. Ask yourself, "If models get ten times better in the next eighteen months, does my company get better or does it get obsoleted?" You want to be building the thing that rides the wave, not the thing that's patching a weakness the next model release will fix for free. The best founders I talk to are the ones who are almost hoping the foundation models improve faster, because every improvement makes their product more valuable.

r001.rationale: The response says the gap between a research paper and a usable product has shortened, but does not say recent papers are becoming more practically oriented rather than theoretical.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about this is that research papers and open-source releases are basically a map of where the frontier is moving, and the trick for a founder is to read that map differently than a researcher would.

A researcher reads a paper and asks, "What's the next incremental thing I can push on?" A founder should read the same paper and ask, "What just became possible that was impossible eighteen months ago, and who has been suffering because it was impossible?" Those are very different questions. The capability is the supply side. The suffering is the demand side. The business lives at the intersection.

A few concrete heuristics I'd give.

First, go where the benchmark numbers are climbing fast but the deployed products are still bad. That gap is the opportunity. If a capability is sitting at ninety-five percent on some academic eval but nobody has built a reliable product on top of it, that usually means the last mile is hard in a way that's not glamorous enough for a paper, which is exactly the kind of work a startup can own. Things like data curation, evaluation harnesses, the boring reliability engineering. That's where the moat actually is, not in the model architecture.

Second, treat open-source models as a starting point, not a product. Download Llama or Qwen or whatever's current, fine-tune it, and you have something that looks like a product in a weekend. That's great for finding signal. But if the open weights are the whole value, you have no value, because everyone else downloaded the same weights. What you want is a flywheel where the product generates data that the open-source base model doesn't have. Proprietary data in a domain that's underrepresented on the internet. Robotics is my obvious example, because the internet is full of text and video but nearly empty of action data, of what a robot's motors actually did. Any physical-world domain has this property. So does a lot of enterprise work.

Third, I'd actually tell founders to pay attention to what the big labs are not doing. The frontier labs are optimizing for the general case because that's where the leverage is for them. They're not going to build the vertical thing for agriculture or dentistry or industrial inspection. The gap between a general foundation model and a specific messy workflow is enormous, and that gap is defensible precisely because it's unsexy.

And one more thing I'd say, which is more of a mindset point. Don't pick a problem just because a paper made it tractable. Pick a problem you'd be willing to spend five years on, and then use the research to figure out whether now is the right moment. Timing matters a lot in this field. A lot of ideas that failed in 2019 are suddenly trivially feasible, and a lot of ideas that look feasible on a demo today still won't work reliably for two or three years. Reading the research closely is how you tell those apart.

r001.rationale: The response discusses using research papers to identify newly possible capabilities, but does not say that recent AI papers are becoming more practically oriented rather than primarily theoretical.

astra-6.text:
I’d start with a problem people already care about, and then work backward to the research. What’s a task that someone spends hours on every week? What makes it difficult, and what would a useful solution actually look like?

Then use open-source tools to test your assumptions quickly. Build the simplest version you can, put it in front of a user, and see where it fails. Those failures can tell you much more than a benchmark score. Maybe the model is capable enough, but it doesn’t have the right context. Maybe it can do individual steps, but it can’t reliably finish the workflow.

Research is useful because it changes what’s feasible. A problem that was out of reach six months ago might now be worth trying. But a new capability isn’t automatically a product. The opportunity is connecting that capability to a real need—and doing the work to make it reliable enough that somebody depends on it.

r001.rationale: The response says research can change what is feasible, but does not state that recent AI papers are becoming more practically oriented rather than primarily theoretical.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d start with a problem where you can get a very clear signal that you’re making someone’s life better. What is a task people do every day that is expensive, repetitive, or frustrating? Then work backward to the research and tools that could help you solve it.

Open source is great for testing those ideas quickly. You can take an existing model, build a prototype, and put it in front of users before investing heavily in training your own system. But look closely at where it fails. Does it need better data? Does it need access to a tool? Does it need to understand a particular workflow? Those failures can tell you where the valuable work is.

I’d also read research with an eye toward what has just become possible. A new capability can unlock a product that wasn’t practical six months ago. The key is connecting that capability to a real need. A compelling demo gets someone’s attention; reliably solving their problem gets them to keep using it.

r001.rationale: The response recommends reading research for newly possible capabilities, but it does not say recent AI papers are becoming more practically oriented or less theoretical.
